body: Malmendier and Tate measure overconfidence by revealed behaviour: a CEO who keeps highly in-the-money options until expiry ('Longholder'), or is described as 'confident/optimistic' in the press, believes their own firm is undervalued. 'CEO Overconfidence and Corporate Investment' (Journal of Finance 60(6), 2005; Forbes 500 firms 1980-1994): investment by overconfident CEOs is much more sensitive to internal cash flow, especially in equity-dependent firms, because they see external equity as too expensive and over-invest when cash is plentiful. 'Who Makes Acquisitions? CEO Overconfidence and the Market's Reaction' (Journal of Financial Economics 89(1), 2008; ~2,980 S2 citations): overconfident CEOs are about 65% more likely to complete a merger, especially diversifying deals financed with cash. The announcement reaction to their bids averages about -90 basis points, versus about -12 for other CEOs. Replicated: yes; many follow-ups (Hirshleifer-Low-Teoh 2012 find that overconfident CEOs also innovate more). Use for us: in India, the founder-promoter with unchecked confidence is common, and the warning signs are diversification into unrelated businesses, cash-funded acquisitions abroad, capex announced at cycle peaks, and refusal to cut capex when returns fall. Pair with Buffett's institutional imperative. Score capital allocation by what was DONE with cash in past cycles, not by how persuasive the CEO sounds. Note the upside: the same trait drives innovation and turnarounds, so it is a sizing and leverage risk, not an automatic exclusion.
title: CEO overconfidence (Malmendier-Tate 2005, 2008): overconfident CEOs over-invest from cash and are 65% more likely to acquire; the market punishes their deals
